sections.title: Why architecture is a security decision
content: Who secures what in the cloud
Special environments: IoT, SCADA, RTOS, embedded, containers, serverless
Where firewalls, proxies and sensors sit
Fail open or fail closed
Modern network ideas and secure protocol swaps
examples: Every server you put on the internet adds to the attack surface
say: Today is about design choices. Each time an organisation picks a cloud model, connects a smart device or puts a server in front of the public, it changes how much an attacker can reach.
That reachable area is called the attack surface. Good architecture shrinks it, and careless architecture grows it without anyone noticing.
The exam loves short scenario questions here, so we will keep asking one thing: who is responsible, and where should the control sit?

checks.question: In your own words, what is an attack surface?
checks.expect: Everything exposed that an attacker could reach or target; design choices make it bigger or smaller.

sections.title: Shared responsibility and the cloud stack
content: Shared responsibility: security duties split between provider and customer
SaaS: you manage data and user access only
PaaS: you manage applications and data
IaaS: you manage the OS, applications and data
Confusion over the split is a listed vulnerability
examples: Microsoft 365 is SaaS: the provider patches everything, but you still decide who gets an account and what is shared
say: In the cloud, security is never handed over completely. The provider and the customer each own a slice, and the size of your slice depends on the service you buy.

Picture a stack of layers from the physical building up to your data. With software as a service, the provider runs almost the whole stack. With infrastructure as a service, you take over the operating system and everything above it.

Notice what never moves: your data and who can access it are always yours. When a company assumes the provider is handling something it is not, settings get left open, and that gap is exactly where breaches happen.
sections.analogy: Software as a service is a fully furnished serviced apartment, platform as a service is a house with walls and a roof that you furnish, and infrastructure as a service is an empty plot where you build. It breaks down because even in infrastructure as a service the provider still supplies the physical servers, network and virtualisation, so the plot already has utilities connected.

checks.question: Which cloud model gives the customer the most control, and what extra work comes with that?
checks.expect: IaaS; the customer must manage and patch the operating system, applications and data.

checks.question: Name one thing the customer is responsible for in every cloud model.
checks.expect: Their data, and user access to it.

misconceptions.belief: If we move to a cloud service, the provider takes care of all the security for us.
misconceptions.correction: The provider secures its part of the stack, but the customer always keeps responsibility for its data and access settings, and more besides in platform or infrastructure services.

sections.title: Special environments
content: IoT: weak authentication, default credentials, rarely patched, so segment it
SCADA and ICS: industrial control, attacks cause physical damage
RTOS: real-time systems where availability comes first
Embedded: built-in computers that cannot run security agents
Containers share the host kernel; serverless still leaves you the code and permissions
examples: Stuxnet damaged industrial centrifuges by attacking their control systems
A smart TV on the staff network is a stepping stone; on its own segment it is contained
say: Some systems cannot be protected the normal way. Smart devices ship with factory passwords and rarely get updates, so the safe answer is nearly always to put them on their own separate network.
Industrial control systems run power plants and factories. A successful attack there does not just leak data, it can break real machinery, which is why Stuxnet is the famous example.

Real-time operating systems run things like medical devices and aircraft, where a delay can cost lives, so availability beats everything. Embedded devices like printers often cannot take an antivirus agent, so you protect the network around them instead.

Containers are lighter than virtual machines because they share the host's kernel, which also means weaker isolation and a risk of escape. With serverless, the provider runs the servers, but your code and its permissions are still yours to secure.

checks.question: Why are containers considered less isolated than virtual machines?
checks.expect: They share the host operating system kernel, so a container escape can affect the host and other containers.

checks.question: For a real-time system in a hospital, which part of the CIA triad usually comes first, and why?
checks.expect: Availability, because a delay or outage could harm patients.

misconceptions.belief: Serverless means there is nothing left for us to secure.
misconceptions.correction: The provider runs the infrastructure, but the customer still owns the code it deploys and the permissions that code is given.

sections.title: The screened subnet and where appliances sit
content: Screened subnet (DMZ): public servers between two firewalls
Jump server: the single audited door for admin access
Forward proxy filters outbound; reverse proxy filters inbound
WAF sits in front of web servers specifically
IDS or IPS sits inside, behind the firewall
examples: Internet, then firewall, then DMZ with web, mail and DNS servers, then firewall, then the internal network
Load balancer: active-active uses every node for speed; active-passive keeps a standby, which is cheaper
say: Think of a bank. The street outside is the internet, the public banking hall is the screened subnet, and the vault is the internal network. Customers can walk into the hall, but a second locked door keeps them out of the vault.
Administrators should not connect straight to servers from anywhere. They go through one hardened jump server, so every admin session passes one point that is logged and watched.
To tell the proxies apart, follow the direction. A forward proxy sits in front of your users going out to the internet. A reverse proxy sits in front of your servers, taking requests coming in.

A web application firewall is the specialist for websites, so it goes directly in front of web servers. Intrusion detection and prevention sensors go behind the main firewall, where they inspect the traffic that made it through.

checks.question: Staff browsing needs filtering so they cannot reach malicious sites. Which kind of proxy do you need?
checks.expect: A forward proxy, because it handles outbound traffic from users to the internet.

checks.question: Why does a screened subnet use two firewalls rather than one?
checks.expect: So public-facing servers are reachable from the internet but a second barrier still protects the internal network if one of them is compromised.

misconceptions.belief: A reverse proxy is just a proxy that protects users while they browse.
misconceptions.correction: That is the forward proxy; a reverse proxy faces the internet on behalf of your servers and filters the requests coming in to them.

sections.title: Fail open or fail closed
content: Fail open: device dies, traffic keeps flowing
Fail closed: device dies, traffic is blocked
Fail open puts availability first and risks security
Fail closed puts security first and risks availability
examples: A fire door that unlocks in a power cut fails open so people can escape
A firewall guarding a payments database should fail closed
say: Every inline security device will break one day, and the design question is what happens to traffic when it does. Either it carries on unchecked, or everything stops.
Neither is always right. If keeping the service running matters most, you let it fail open. If letting unchecked traffic through is unacceptable, you let it fail closed and accept the outage.
In a question, look for the clue about priorities. Words like life safety or must stay online point one way, while sensitive data or must never be exposed point the other.

checks.question: An intrusion prevention system protecting card payment data loses power. Should it fail open or closed, and what is the cost?
checks.expect: Fail closed to protect the data; the cost is lost availability until it is fixed.

sections.title: Modern network concepts and secure protocols
content: VLAN: logical separation on shared hardware
802.1X: devices authenticate before joining
SD-WAN: software-managed WAN over internet links, must be encrypted
SASE: networking and security as one cloud service
Microsegmentation: every workload isolated, zero-trust style
examples: HTTP 80 to HTTPS 443, Telnet 23 to SSH 22, FTP 21 to SFTP 22 or FTPS 990
LDAP 389 to LDAPS 636, SNMP v1 or v2 to SNMPv3, DNS to DNS over HTTPS
say: Virtual networks let one switch behave like several separate ones, which makes segmentation cheap. Port-based authentication goes further: a device must prove who it is before it gets on at all, which beats filtering by hardware address, because those addresses are easy to fake.

Software-defined wide area networking links branch offices over ordinary internet connections instead of expensive private lines, so the traffic has to be encrypted. Secure access service edge, pronounced sassy, bundles networking and security into a single service delivered from the cloud.
Microsegmentation takes isolation down to each individual workload, so one compromised server cannot freely talk to its neighbours.
For protocols, learn the swaps as pairs. If a question shows an old clear-text protocol, the answer is its encrypted replacement, and the port numbers often give it away.

checks.question: Why is port-based authentication stronger than allowing devices by their hardware address?
checks.expect: MAC addresses can be spoofed, whereas 802.1X makes the device authenticate before it joins.

checks.question: An admin still manages switches with Telnet. What should replace it, and on which port?
checks.expect: SSH on port 22, because it encrypts the session including credentials.

misconceptions.belief: SNMP version 3 needs a different port from the older versions.
misconceptions.correction: Version 3 still uses port 161; the improvement is that it adds authentication and encryption, not a new port.

sections.title: Design a small company network
content: Decide who owns each risk
Choose where each device goes
Pick fail open or fail closed with a reason
examples: Web shop servers go in the DMZ; the customer database stays internal
say: Let us put this together. You will see a small company scenario on screen in a moment; talk me through your design one piece at a time. There is no single perfect answer, but every choice needs a reason.
Start with the easy wins: what is public, what is private, and which devices cannot defend themselves.

checks.question: Where would you put the company's public web server, and what would sit directly in front of it?
checks.expect: In the screened subnet, with a web application firewall in front of it.

application.scenario: A small online retailer runs its shop on rented virtual servers it patches itself, keeps a customer database in the office, has smart CCTV cameras with default passwords, and its IT contractor logs in from home to manage servers.
application.question: Which cloud model is the shop using and what must the retailer patch, where do the cameras go, and how should the contractor get admin access?
application.expect: IaaS, so the retailer patches the OS and apps and owns data and access; put the cameras on their own segmented network or VLAN and change default credentials; route contractor admin access through a single audited jump server rather than direct connections.

sections.title: Key distinctions and traps
content: Data and access are always the customer's job
Containers share a kernel; VMs do not
Forward is outbound, reverse is inbound
Fail open favours availability, fail closed favours security
VLANs separate; 802.1X makes devices prove themselves first
examples: Cleartext protocol in the question? Pick its encrypted partner
say: Three traps catch people here. Believing the cloud provider does everything, mixing up the two proxies, and forgetting that containers share a kernel.
When a question describes a fragile device that cannot be patched or run an agent, the answer is almost always to isolate it on its own network.
And for any failure question, ask what the scenario values more, staying online or staying safe, then pick the failure mode that matches.

checks.question: Which device would you place directly in front of a public website to stop attacks such as injection?
In platform as a service, what does the customer manage?
checks.expect: Its applications and data, plus user access.

retrieval.question: What do you already know about the difference between software, platform and infrastructure as a service?
retrieval.expect: SaaS is a ready-made application, PaaS is a platform to deploy your own apps, IaaS is raw virtual servers you manage.

retrieval.question: What does a firewall do, in one sentence?
retrieval.expect: It allows or blocks network traffic according to rules.

exam_questions.q: In a cloud model, which party is responsible for more of the underlying infrastructure?
options: The provider as the service moves toward SaaS
exam_questions.answer: The provider as the service moves toward SaaS
exam_questions.why: The provider takes on more of the stack the more managed the service is: least in IaaS, most in SaaS, where the customer keeps only data and user access.

exam_questions.q: Why is cloud misconfiguration a major security concern?
options: A misconfigured service can expose resources despite otherwise strong controls
exam_questions.answer: A misconfigured service can expose resources despite otherwise strong controls
exam_questions.why: Under shared responsibility the customer owns its settings and access, so one wrong setting, such as a publicly readable storage bucket, can expose data even when the provider's own security is strong.

exam_questions.q: Which network concept places security controls according to where traffic must be inspected or enforced?
exam_questions.why: Placement means putting each control where the traffic it must handle actually passes, such as a WAF in front of web servers or a reverse proxy facing inbound requests.

added_facts: In IaaS the provider still supplies physical hardware, networking and virtualisation (used to say where the empty-plot analogy breaks down).
Misconfiguration, such as a publicly readable storage bucket, is the typical result of shared-responsibility confusion (used in the exam explanation).
Spoofable MAC addresses are why 802.1X beats MAC filtering (notes say spoofable, made explicit).
SNMPv3 keeps port 161 and adds authentication and encryption.
A WAF defends against web attacks such as injection.
Fire doors unlocking in a power cut as a fail-open example; CIA triad named in a check.
exam_changes: Question 1: the pack answer said the provider takes on more 'as the service moves toward IaaS', which is backwards; changed the option and answer to 'toward SaaS'.
All three 'why' lines rewritten as student explanations.
